questions.question: Which point belongs to $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}((0,0),1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the usual distance?
In the Euclidean metric, how is a closed metric ball related to the corresponding open metric ball?
options: It is always disjoint from the corresponding open metric ball.
It is always smaller than the corresponding open metric ball.
It has no relation to the corresponding open metric ball.
It is the closure of the corresponding open metric ball.

questions.question: What inequality defines membership in $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)$?
options: $d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \lt r$
$d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)\le r$
$d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0) \gt r$
$d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_0)=0$ only

questions.question: What does a closed metric ball include that an open ball of the same radius may exclude?
options: Points at exact distance $r$ from the centre
Points at distance less than $r$ from the centre
Points at distance up to $2r$ from the centre
Points at distance greater than $r$ from the centre

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual distance, what is $\overline B(0,2)$?
Does $(3/5,4/5)$ belong to $\overline{\boldsymbol{B}}((0,0),1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: Yes, its distance from the origin is $1$.
No, its distance from the origin is greater than $1$.
No, points at exact radius are excluded.
Yes, because every point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ belongs to the unit ball.

questions.question: Let $(X,d)$ be any metric space, $x_0\in X$ and $r>0$. Which statement about the closed ball $\overline{B}(x_0,r)$ holds in every metric space?
options: It is a closed set.
It is the closure of the open ball $B(x_0,r)$.
It is not an open set.
It contains a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x_0$.

questions.question: Let $(X,d)$ be an arbitrary metric space, $x_0\in X$ and $r>0$. How are the closure $\overline{B(x_0,r)}$ of the open ball and the closed ball $\overline{B}(x_0,r)$ related?
options: $\overline{B(x_0,r)}\subseteq\overline{B}(x_0,r)$ always, and the inclusion can be strict.
$\overline{B(x_0,r)}=\overline{B}(x_0,r)$ always.
$\overline{B}(x_0,r)\subseteq\overline{B(x_0,r)}$ always, and the inclusion can be strict.
Neither set need be contained in the other.

questions.question: Which hypothesis on the metric space $(X,d)$ guarantees that $\overline{B}(x_0,r)$ equals the closure of the open ball $B(x_0,r)$ for every centre $x_0$ and every radius $r>0$?
options: $X$ is a normed vector space and $d$ is the metric induced by its norm.
$X=\mathbb{R}^n$ and $d$ is topologically equivalent to the Euclidean metric.
The closed ball $\overline{B}(x_0,r)$ is a closed set.
Every open ball $B(x_0,r)$ is a non-empty open set.

questions.question: Let $d$ be the discrete metric on a set $X$ with at least two points ($d(x,y)=1$ for $x\neq y$ and $d(x,x)=0$), and fix $x_0\in X$. Which pair of equalities is correct?
options: $B(x_0,1)=X$ and $\overline{B}(x_0,1)=X$.
$B(x_0,1)=\varnothing$ and $\overline{B}(x_0,1)=\{x_0\}$.

questions.question: In a metric space $(X,d)$ let $y\notin\overline{B}(x_0,r)$, so $d(y,x_0)>r$. Which choice of $s>0$ guarantees, for every such $y$, that the open ball $B(y,s)$ is disjoint from $\overline{B}(x_0,r)$?
options: $s=r$
